To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

following global ischemia there is a ten-fold increase in the birth rate of new neurons in the subgranual zone of dentate granule cell layer, that 60% of these newborn neurons migrate into the granular cell layer where they mature and integrate into hippocampal circuitry and that 25% of newborn cells migrate into the hilus and mature to become astrocytes.

following global ischemia there is an increased birth of new neurons in the subgranolar zone that migrate into the dentatate granule cell layer and hilus where a proportion become mature neurons and glia.

ischemia induces the proliferation of cells in the adult dentate gyrus, and that a large fraction of the cells born following ischemia differentiate into mature neurons that are incorporated into the granule neuron layer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of ischemia on the hippocampus.
the role of ischemia-induced neuroplasticity in functional recovery.
the study of the mechanisms that control the birth, migration, and differentiation of cells in the adult brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
neurogenesis is a normal process in the adult brain that is enhanced by ischemia and other insults, and that this process may serve to repair the damage caused by the insult.
ischemia-induced neuronal cell death is followed by a compensatory response that includes a robust increase in neurogenesis.
ischemia-induced hippocampal neurogenesis is an important mechanism of recovery following ischemia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

neurogenesis is increased in the dentate subgranular zone following global cerebral ischemia, and the new neurons that are generated migrate into the granular cell layer and differentiate into mature neurons that may contribute to the recovery of memory following cerebral ischemia.
ischemia-induced adult neurogenesis is a dynamic process that is highly sensitive to the timing and severity of the insult, the duration of the ischemia, and the age of the animal.
ischemic neurogenesis may be a mechanism to restore function in the adult brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the adult brain is capable of generating new neurons, which may be important to recovery from brain injury.
the adult brain has an innate ability to repair itself following injury.
the adult brain retains the capacity to generate new cells following brain injury and that these newborn cells can integrate into existing neuronal circuits and contribute to recovery of function.
